summary: Defines Proxy Mobile IPv6, a network-based mobility protocol. The network tracks the host's movement and does the signaling for it, so the host needs no mobility software. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Proxy Mobile IPv6 lets a network manage an IPv6 host's movement between access links. The network updates its routing while the host keeps using its home network address.

questions: what is a local mobility anchor
what is a mobile access gateway
proxy binding update vs binding update
subtitle: A network tracks an IPv6 host as it moves, so the host does not send mobility updates.

tldr.problem: Mobile IPv6 asks a host to signal its home agent whenever it moves. Some networks need mobility support for hosts that do not perform this signaling.
tldr.mechanism: A Mobile Access Gateway detects attachment and sends a Proxy Binding Update to a Local Mobility Anchor. They establish a tunnel and preserve the host's home network prefix across access links.
tldr.outcome: The host can retain its address while moving within the domain, without taking part in mobility signaling. RFC 5213 has been updated by RFC 6543 and RFC 7864.

today: RFC 5213 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 6543 and RFC 7864. The metadata does not list a document that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Mobility Managed by the Network
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 uses messages from a host, called a mobile node, to keep its home address reachable as it moves. RFC 5213 defines another approach: the network sends those mobility messages on the host's behalf.

The protocol is called Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6). It extends Mobile IPv6 signaling and home-agent functions, so the host does not need to participate in mobility signaling. The RFC describes mobility for IPv6 prefixes over an IPv6 transport network.
sections.plainLanguage: The network tracks where a host connects and updates its own routing. The host does not have to send mobility messages when it moves.

sections.title: The Local Mobility Anchor and Access Gateway
sections.content:
A PMIPv6 domain contains a Local Mobility Anchor (LMA) and one or more Mobile Access Gateways (MAGs). The LMA acts as the mobile node's home agent and keeps its binding state. A MAG runs on an access router, detects a node's movement on its access link, and signals the LMA.

The LMA anchors the node's home network prefix. The MAG advertises that prefix on the access link, so the node can configure an address from it. This specification supports a separate prefix or prefix set for each node; it does not support sharing a prefix among nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: The LMA keeps the node's home prefix reachable. Each MAG detects the node on its local link and tells the LMA when the node attaches or moves.

sections.title: Registration and Handoff
sections.content:
When a node attaches, its MAG identifies it and checks whether the network authorizes mobility service. The MAG sends a Proxy Binding Update (PBU) to the LMA. If accepted, the LMA creates a binding entry, assigns or confirms the node's home network prefix, sets up its tunnel end, and replies with a Proxy Binding Acknowledgement (PBA).

The MAG establishes its tunnel end and advertises the home prefix in Router Advertisements. During a handoff, the old MAG can request de-registration. The LMA waits for a limited period before deleting the binding, allowing a registration from the new MAG to update it. The new MAG advertises the same prefix so the node can retain its address configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: After attachment, the MAG asks the LMA to register the node and receives its home prefix. At a new access link, another MAG registers the node so it can keep that prefix.

sections.title: Tunnels Carry the Node's Traffic
sections.content:
The LMA advertises a route for the node's home prefix and forwards packets for that prefix through a bi-directional tunnel to the serving MAG. The MAG removes the outer tunnel header and delivers the packet on the access link. In the reverse direction, the MAG sends the node's packets through the tunnel to the LMA, which removes the outer header and routes them onward.

RFC 5213 specifies IPv6-in-IPv6 tunneling for an IPv6 transport network. The MAG acts as the node's default router. If a correspondent node is connected to the same MAG, the MAG may route traffic locally instead of sending it through the LMA.
sections.plainLanguage: The LMA forwards incoming packets through a tunnel to the MAG serving the node. The MAG sends the node's outgoing packets through the tunnel to the LMA.

sections.title: Binding Messages and Their Options
sections.content:
A PBU is a Mobile IPv6 Binding Update sent by a MAG to an LMA. RFC 5213 adds a Proxy Registration flag, which is set for proxy registrations. The matching PBA reports whether the LMA accepted the update; status values below 128 indicate acceptance, and values at or above 128 indicate rejection.

The messages can carry the mobile node identifier, one or more home network prefixes, a handoff indicator, access technology, a timestamp, a link-layer identifier, and a link-local address. The LMA and MAG must skip mobility options they do not understand. The Home Network Prefix option uses type 22 and contains a 16-byte IPv6 prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: The MAG and LMA exchange binding messages that identify the node and its home prefix. The reply reports whether the registration succeeded.

sections.title: Protecting Signaling and Authorizing Gateways
sections.content:
The PBU and PBA messages between a MAG and LMA must have integrity protection and data-origin authentication. Both entities must implement IPsec. The RFC recommends ESP in transport mode with integrity protection and recommends IKEv2 for setting up security associations; confidentiality for these signaling messages is not required.

The LMA must restrict proxy bindings to MAGs and prefixes that it has authorized through local configuration. The access network is also expected to authenticate and authorize the mobile node before granting network access. Without these checks, an attacker could take over a mobility session or cause denial of service.
sections.plainLanguage: The MAG and LMA must verify each other's signaling messages. The LMA must also authorize which gateways can register each node and prefix.
